title: Conditional Probability

intro.body:
**Conditional probability** answers the question: *given that one event has already happened, how likely is another?* We write $P(A \mid B)$ — read "the probability of $A$ given $B$."

The key idea is that knowing $B$ occurred **shrinks the sample space**. We no longer look at everyone — we look only at the outcomes inside $B$, and ask what fraction of *those* are also in $A$:

$$P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} = \frac{\#(A \cap B)}{\#(B)}$$

When the data come from counts, the probabilities of $A\cap B$ and $B$ share the same denominator (the total number of people), so it cancels — you can work directly with the **counts**: divide the number of outcomes in *both* $A$ and $B$ by the number of outcomes in $B$.

**Worked example.** A gym surveys 40 members about whether they swim and whether they do yoga:

| | Yoga | No yoga | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Swim** | 8 | 12 | 20 |
| **No swim** | 6 | 14 | 20 |
| **Total** | 14 | 26 | 40 |

To find $P(\text{Yoga} \mid \text{Swim})$, restrict to the **20 swimmers** (the row where Swim is true) — they are the new sample space. Of those 20, exactly **8** also do yoga. So
$$P(\text{Yoga} \mid \text{Swim}) = \frac{8}{20} = \frac{2}{5}.$$
Notice we divided by 20 (the swimmers), **not** by 40 (everyone). Conditioning on "Swim" threw away the 20 non-swimmers entirely.

problem_generator.description: Two-way count table on two yes/no attributes (owns a dog = B, plays a sport = A). All four cells are positive integers; #(A∩B) < #(B) so P(A|B) is a proper non-integer fraction, and #(A∩B) shares a factor > 1 with #(B) so the final fraction genuinely reduces to lowest terms.
problem_generator.display_problem: A school surveys its students about two things: whether they own a dog and whether they play a sport. The results: ${both}$ students own a dog **and** play a sport; ${dog_only}$ own a dog but do **not** play a sport; ${sport_only}$ play a sport but do **not** own a dog; and ${neither}$ do neither. Find $P(\text{plays a sport} \mid \text{owns a dog})$ — the probability that a randomly chosen dog owner plays a sport.

steps.title: Count everyone surveyed
steps.prompt: Start with the full picture. Adding up all four groups — {both} (dog and sport), {dog_only} (dog only), {sport_only} (sport only), and {neither} (neither) — how many students were surveyed in total?

wrong_answer_feedback.feedback: {count_B} is just the dog owners ({both} + {dog_only}). The total also includes students without a dog. Add all four groups: {both} + {dog_only} + {sport_only} + {neither} = {grand_total}.
{count_A} counts only the sport players. Include everyone: {both} + {dog_only} + {sport_only} + {neither} = {grand_total}.

steps.title: Restrict to the conditioning event B
steps.prompt: We want $P(\text{sport} \mid \text{dog})$, so we condition on owning a dog: we look only at dog owners. This restricted group is our new sample space. How many students own a dog?
steps.hint: The dog owners are the {both} who also play a sport plus the {dog_only} who don't: {both} + {dog_only}.

wrong_answer_feedback.feedback: {grand_total} is everyone surveyed. But conditioning on "owns a dog" throws away the students without a dog — the new sample space is only the dog owners: {both} + {dog_only} = {count_B}.
{both} is the dog owners who ALSO play a sport, not all dog owners. Every dog owner counts here, whether or not they play a sport: {both} + {dog_only} = {count_B}.
The dog owners are those who play a sport plus those who don't: {both} + {dog_only} = {count_B}.

steps.title: Count A and B together
steps.prompt: Now, inside that group of {count_B} dog owners, how many also play a sport? This is $\#(A \cap B)$ — the students who own a dog **and** play a sport.
steps.hint: You need students who are in BOTH categories at once — own a dog and play a sport. That count is given directly in the problem.

wrong_answer_feedback.feedback: {count_A} is every sport player in the whole school, including {sport_only} who don't own a dog. We've already restricted to dog owners, so count only the dog owners who play a sport: {both}.
{count_B} is ALL dog owners. We want just the dog owners who also play a sport — the overlap of the two groups: {both}.
$\#(A \cap B)$ is the count in both categories at once — own a dog and play a sport: {both}.

steps.title: Simplify: find the GCF
steps.prompt: So $P(\text{sport} \mid \text{dog}) = \dfrac{\#(A \cap B)}{\#(B)} = \frac{{{both}}}{{{count_B}}}$. Before writing this in lowest terms, find the greatest common factor (GCF) of {both} and {count_B}.
steps.hint: What is the largest number that divides both {both} and {count_B} evenly?

wrong_answer_feedback.feedback: A GCF of 1 would mean the fraction is already in lowest terms, but {both} and {count_B} do share a larger common factor. Their greatest common factor is {gcf}.

wrong_answer_feedback.condition: answer_int is not None and answer_int > 1 and both % answer_int == 0 and count_B % answer_int == 0 and answer_int < gcf
wrong_answer_feedback.feedback: {answer} divides both {both} and {count_B}, but it isn't the GREATEST such factor. Look for a larger one — the GCF is {gcf}.
The greatest common factor of {both} and {count_B} is {gcf}.

steps.title: Write the probability in simplest form
steps.prompt: Divide the numerator and denominator of $\frac{{{both}}}{{{count_B}}}$ by the GCF {gcf}. Write $P(\text{sport} \mid \text{dog})$ as a fraction in simplest form.

strict_form.rejection_feedback: That value is correct, but it isn't a fully simplified fraction. Divide both {both} and {count_B} by their GCF {gcf} to get $\frac{{{simp_num}}}{{{simp_den}}}$.

steps.hint: Compute {both} ÷ {gcf} for the numerator and {count_B} ÷ {gcf} for the denominator, then write the result as a fraction.

wrong_answer_feedback.feedback: Divide top and bottom by {gcf}: {both} ÷ {gcf} = {simp_num} and {count_B} ÷ {gcf} = {simp_den}, so $\frac{{{both}}}{{{count_B}}} = \frac{{{simp_num}}}{{{simp_den}}}$. Enter it as a fraction. (Remember: divide by $\#(B) = {count_B}$, the dog owners — not by the {grand_total} total students.)

steps.title: Check your understanding
steps.prompt: When we compute $P(A \mid B)$ — the probability of playing a sport given owning a dog — what does "conditioning on $B$" actually do?
options: It restricts attention to the outcomes in B only. The dog owners become the new, smaller sample space, and we ask what fraction of them are also in A.
It asks, out of all students surveyed, what fraction both own a dog and play a sport.
It adds the probability of owning a dog to the probability of playing a sport, since both can happen.
steps.hint: We divided by the number of dog owners, not by the total number of students. What did conditioning do to the group we were looking at?

wrong_answer_feedback.feedback: That describes $P(A \cap B)$ — the joint probability over EVERYONE, dividing by the {grand_total} total. Conditional probability instead divides by only the {count_B} dog owners: conditioning shrinks the sample space to B.

Adding probabilities isn't what conditioning does. $P(A \mid B)$ restricts the sample space to just the dog owners (B) and asks what fraction of them are in A — that's why we divided by {count_B}, not the total.
The first option is correct: conditioning on B discards everything outside B, making the {count_B} dog owners the new sample space, and asks what fraction of them also play a sport.

completion_message: You found $P(\text{plays a sport} \mid \text{owns a dog})$ by restricting to the {count_B} dog owners and asking how many of them — {both} — also play a sport: $\frac{{{both}}}{{{count_B}}} = \frac{{{simp_num}}}{{{simp_den}}}$. The key move was conditioning: shrinking the sample space from all {grand_total} students down to just B. Ready to practice?
